title: Connecting two apps that don't talk to each other
promise: You're going to set up two connections that run on their own. The first: emails you care about land row by row in a spreadsheet. The second: every form someone submits shows up in a Slack channel in under five seconds. No duplicates. And an email alert the day it breaks.
why: Ruben repairs and sells used bikes in Granada. Orders from his site arrive by email with the subject "New order #1044." He copies them by hand into a spreadsheet: name, model, amount, address. About 43 a week. Each one takes him two minutes with interruptions: almost an hour and a half of his Sunday. In March he missed two orders because they arrived while he was truing a wheel. One of them was for $620. What he needed wasn't to learn to code. It was forty minutes to build the pipe running from email to spreadsheet. And to know why the first time it wrote the same order fourteen times in a row.

theory.title: No app has a door into the one next door
theory.text: Gmail doesn't know your spreadsheet exists. And your form has no idea what Slack is. It's nobody's negligence: every application is a closed box, with its data inside. It only has one slit through which it can be talked to from outside. That slit is called an API: the window where one program serves another program, not a person with a mouse and keyboard. When you say "I want to connect Gmail to my spreadsheet," what's actually needed is a third party. Something that's listening, that goes to Gmail's window to pick up, and goes to the spreadsheet's window to drop off. That third party is the real work, and it's the only thing you're going to build today. And here's the question nagging you: do I have to code it myself? No. You're going to dictate it to the AI in a long prompt and it writes the thirty lines. But you have to know what you're asking for. If you don't know what the three links are, you won't be able to tell it what's failing.
theory.analogy: It's two houses built wall to wall, with no door between them. To carry an envelope from one to the other you have to go out to the street. You ring the neighbor's doorbell and wait for someone to open. Being next to each other doesn't help at all.
theory.example: Ruben had his two houses: Gmail with 43 emails a week and a Google sheet with six columns. What he did on Sundays — open the email, read, switch tabs, type — was exactly the third party's job. A human was doing it with a coffee next to them, and that's why he sometimes missed one.

theory.title: The three links: trigger, data, and action
theory.text: Every connection, the dumbest one and the most expensive one, has the same shape: something happens, some data is collected, something is done with it. The trigger (the "something happens") comes in two flavors, and it's worth knowing which one applies to you. First flavor: the source app notifies you the instant it happens; that's a webhook and it's immediate. Second flavor: nobody notifies you and you have to go check every X minutes; that's called polling and it arrives with a delay. Gmail doesn't notify you: you have to go look. That's why Ruben's setup takes up to ten minutes to show. A form can notify instantly, which is why the Slack message arrives in three seconds. In between is the data. An email isn't "an email": it's a list of named fields — date, sender, subject, body, ID. You have to decide which ones cross to the other side and in what order. The action is the finish line: writing a row, sending a message, creating a task. Get in the habit of saying out loud "what comes in, what changes, what goes out" before touching anything. It'll save you half the failures: almost all of them are a field you thought was coming through and wasn't.
theory.analogy: The webhook is the doorbell: it rings and you go. Polling is peeking out the window every ten minutes to see if anyone's arrived. Both work; one wears out more shoe leather and arrives later.
theory.example: Ruben's three links, written in one line each. Trigger: "an email has arrived whose subject starts with New order and that I haven't processed yet." Data: "date, sender, order number, amount, and message ID." Action: "add a row at the end of the Orders tab." That's the line he pasted to the AI, and that's where the code came from.

theory.title: Credentials: three ways to prove who you are, and you'll only touch two
theory.text: For the third party to get into Gmail it has to prove it has your permission. There are three different ways of doing that, and people confuse them all the time. The first is the API key: a long string of letters you show and that's it, like the ones you use with AI models. The second is OAuth: the "log in with your Google account" system. You don't hand your password to anyone. Google shows you a screen, you click "Allow," and Google hands the program a temporary pass. You can revoke that pass whenever you want from your account. Everything from Google goes through here. The third is the webhook with a secret URL: an extremely long, impossible-to-guess address, and knowing it IS the permission. Slack works this way for what you'll do today. And this has a consequence people miss: that address is as sensitive as a password. Whoever has it can post in your channel even if they don't work with you. No login required and no record of who did it. Don't paste it into the AI's chat. Don't put it in a website's code. And don't show it in a screenshot on a forum asking for help.
theory.analogy: The API key is a loose key. OAuth is the doorman: you tell him to let that gentleman into the machine room. The doorman gives him a badge with a photo. And tomorrow you take the badge back with one call. The secret webhook is a door with no lock in an empty lot: the only thing protecting it is that almost nobody knows where it is.
theory.example: A Slack webhook address looks like this: https://hooks.slack.com/services/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. The three final blocks are the secret. Anyone who copies that entire line can post messages in your channel from home, signed with your app's name.

theory.title: Permissions: the problem isn't that it asks for too much, it's that you don't read it
theory.text: When you authorize your first script, Google will show you a list of sentences. A typical one: "Read, compose, send, and permanently delete all your Gmail." That's called a scope: what the program will be able to do with your account. That particular sentence is scary for a reason. It's the broadest permission there is over your email, and a script that only reads subjects doesn't need half of it. The golden rule is minimum permission. Ask the AI to use read-only and labels if it's not going to send anything. And check that the list doesn't include "delete permanently" if your script doesn't delete anything. Right after, a screen appears saying "Google hasn't verified this app." That's where most people back off and give up. Nothing bad is happening: that unverified app is you. You wrote it thirty seconds ago and it lives inside your own account. Google only verifies things strangers are going to use, and you're not planning to distribute this. Click "Advanced" and then the small link below, "Go to [your project name] (unsafe)." Also save this address, which is your panic button: at myaccount.google.com/permissions you see everything with access to your account. And right there you can pull anyone's pass in two clicks.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between giving the cleaning lady the storage room key or the whole keyring. The keyring includes the mailbox, the garage, and the safe. Both options open the storage room. Only one lets you sleep soundly.
theory.example: The "unverified" warning appears because your project hasn't gone through Google's review. That review takes weeks and is meant for apps with thousands of users. If instead of your own script it were someone else's website showing you that screen, the right move would be to close it. The whole difference is whether you wrote that code a minute ago or someone sent it to you over WhatsApp.

theory.title: The first classic mistake: fourteen identical rows
theory.text: You set it up, it works, you go get lunch. You come back and find the same order written fourteen times. You haven't broken anything: this is what always happens the first time. Your script runs every ten minutes and does exactly what you told it to: it looks for emails matching the condition and writes them. But nobody told it that last round's emails were already written. The email is still in the inbox and still matches the search. So it copies it again every ten minutes, forever. The fix has an ugly name and a simple idea: making it idempotent, which means running it ten times leaves the same result as running it once. It's achieved two ways, and it's worth doing both at once. First: mark what's processed. Give the email a Gmail label called "processed" as soon as the row is written. And exclude that label from the search with a minus sign in front. Second: save each message's unique ID in a spreadsheet column. That way it checks before writing whether it's already there. The first one does the work. The second is the seatbelt, for the day you accidentally delete the label. This bug's evil twin is the opposite, and it's more treacherous: nothing arrives and there's no visible error. It happens because the trigger got saved wrong or was created with a different Google account. That's why the next thing you do after setting something up is never celebrating. It's opening the run log and seeing with your own eyes that it says "Completed."
theory.analogy: It's the PAID stamp on old-school invoices. Without the stamp, every time someone opens the folder they pay the same invoice again and swear it was the first time.
theory.example: Ruben's search before: subject:"New order". Ruben's search after: subject:"New order" -label:processed newer_than:7d. The minus sign in front of label means "not this." And newer_than:7d is the belt for the belt. If one day it gets confused and deletes the labels, at worst it rewrites a week, not four years of email.

theory.title: What to build it with, and how much each path costs
theory.text: There are four paths to the same result. Between the first and the last there's a difference of $0 to $300 a year. The first is Google Apps Script: code that lives inside your own spreadsheet. It's free, no new account, no card, and no giving an outside company access to your Gmail. For anything between Google products — Gmail, Sheets, Forms, Drive, Calendar — it's the right answer. Also for sending alerts to Slack. And almost nobody knows about it. It has a ceiling you won't come close to: each run lasts at most 6 minutes. Also, on a free Gmail account, all your automations combined can't run for more than about 90 minutes a day. The second path is Make, which works with boxes and arrows instead of code. It's free up to about 1,000 operations a month, and the next tier is around $9 a month. The third is Zapier, the easiest of all and the most expensive. It gives about 100 tasks a month on the free plan, which you'll burn through in the first week. Past that you're in the $20-30 a month zone. The fourth is n8n: more powerful and more of a hassle, around $20 a month on its hosted version. Start with the first. And check prices when you're about to pay, because they change every season. Does your connection touch two non-Google services — Stripe with Notion, say? Then yes, look at Make.
theory.example: Ruben's setup, with both connections running: $0.00 a month. The same thing in Zapier would be two Zaps with several steps and about 400 tasks a month counting the forms. The bill: about $29 a month, $348 a year to avoid writing one prompt.

tasks.title: Write your connection as one three-part sentence
tasks.where: On paper, or in ChatGPT's, Claude's, or Gemini's text box
tasks.action: Before opening anything, write the sentence: "When THIS happens, grab THESE FIELDS and do THIS OTHER THING." Be unbearably specific. "When an important email arrives" doesn't count: "when an email arrives whose subject contains New order and that comes from orders@myshop.com" does. If you can't write the sentence, it's not that you're missing technical skill. It's that you don't yet know what you want, and the AI won't guess it for you. Once you have it, paste the prompt below to have it turned into a spec sheet with the exact fields.
tasks.prompt:
You're an automation expert who works with people who have never coded before. Your job is to turn a vague idea into a technical spec sheet a beginner can execute.

I want to connect two applications. Here's what I want to happen:
[WRITE YOUR SENTENCE HERE: when THIS happens, grab THESE FIELDS, and do THIS OTHER THING. With real names of apps, senders, subjects, and sheets.]

Give me a spec sheet with exactly these sections and nothing else:

1) TRIGGER: what specific event kicks it off, and tell me whether the source app can notify on its own the instant it happens or whether I have to go check every X minutes. If checking is needed, recommend how often and why.
2) DATA: the exact list of fields that need to be pulled from the source, with the name each field has in that application. Mark which ones might come back empty some day.
3) ACTION: exactly what gets written or sent to the destination, and in what order.
4) UNIQUE ID: which field tells you whether an item has already been processed, so it's never duplicated.
5) WHAT HAPPENS IF IT FAILS: the three most likely failures for this specific connection, and how I'd notice each one.
6) TOOL: tell me whether this can be done with free Google Apps Script or whether I need a paid tool, and why.

Don't write any code yet. Be direct, no fluff.
tasks.expect: A short spec sheet with six sections. What matters most is point 4. If the AI can't find a unique identifier, it'll tell you. That means you're going to get duplicates no matter what, and it needs solving before moving on.
tasks.stuck: If it hands you back an architecture with databases and message queues, reply: "this is for a company. I'm one person with a spreadsheet. Give me the smallest version that works with what I already have installed." Does it tell you you need paid Zapier for something that only touches Gmail and spreadsheets? Ignore it and move to task 3.

tasks.title: Prepare the destination sheet with the final columns
tasks.action: Create a new sheet and give it a real name, for example "Web orders 2026." At the very bottom, where it says "Sheet1," double-click and rename it "Orders." That name is what the code will use: write it exactly, no weird capitalization or trailing space. In row 1 write the headers that came out of the spec sheet, one per column. Always add one more column at the end called "Message ID," even if you never look at it: it's the one that prevents duplicates. And add another called "Imported on," with the date the row came in. The day something looks off, that column tells you in two seconds whether the problem is from today or has been sitting there three weeks.
tasks.prompt:
I'm setting up a Google spreadsheet where rows will write themselves from my emails.

I'm pasting one of those emails below, with the personal data already swapped for made-up info:
[PASTE A FULL REAL EMAIL HERE: subject and body, swapping names, amounts, and addresses for fake ones]

Tell me:
1) What columns the sheet should have so that email fits in entirely without repeating info. Give me the exact name of each header, short with no odd accents, and the order I'd place them left to right.
2) What format each column should have: text, number, date, or currency.
3) Which of those fields ALWAYS come through in this type of email and which might be missing some day.
4) Which piece of data from this email works as a unique identifier to avoid duplicate rows. If there's none good in the text, say so clearly and propose an alternative.
5) One extra column I'm forgetting that I'll thank myself for in six months.

Don't write code. Just the column table and the answers. Be direct.
tasks.expect: A sheet with the tab named Orders and one header row. For example: Date | Sender | Subject | Order # | Amount | Message ID | Imported on.
tasks.stuck: Unsure which columns to add? Open three real emails you're going to process. Note which piece of data from each you'd want in a table. Whatever isn't in all three emails, leave out. A column that's always empty will cost you half an hour hunting a bug that doesn't exist.

tasks.title: Open the code editor without leaving the sheet
tasks.where: In your Google spreadsheet, in the top menu
tasks.action: In the menu bar — File, Edit, View, Insert, Format... — click "Extensions" and then "Apps Script." A new tab opens with a code editor and a file called Code.gs that comes with an empty function inside. Select everything inside it (Ctrl+A or Cmd+A) and delete it: you're going to paste something else over it. Top left it says "Untitled project": click and rename it "Order importer." That's the name you'll see later on the permissions screen. Also in the list of apps with access to your account. There are four icons on the left sidebar you'll use today. They're the code icon, the clock (Triggers), the list (Executions), and the gear.
tasks.expect: A new browser tab and an editor with a dark or light background. The Code.gs file empty, and the project name changed, top left.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see "Extensions" in the menu, you're in Excel or a read-only view, not Google Sheets. If clicking "Apps Script" does nothing, it's your pop-up blocker. Check the icon to the right of the address bar and allow pop-ups for docs.google.com.

tasks.title: Dictate the code to the AI and paste it as-is
tasks.where: In ChatGPT's, Claude's, or Gemini's text box, then in the Apps Script editor
tasks.action: Fill in the blanks in the prompt below with the details from your spec sheet and your sheet. The more specific you are about the Gmail search and the column order, the fewer round trips you'll make. Copy the entire response — just the code block, not the explanations — and paste it into the Apps Script editor over the empty file. Then click the floppy disk icon or Ctrl+S to save. Don't run it yet.
tasks.prompt:
You're an expert Google Apps Script programmer. You're writing for someone who has never coded and who's going to copy your code as-is, without fully understanding it, so it has to work on the first try and can't depend on anything that needs installing.

I want a script that lives inside my Google spreadsheet and does this:

1) Search my Gmail for messages matching this exact query: [PASTE YOUR SEARCH HERE, e.g.: subject:"New order" -label:processed newer_than:7d]
2) From each message pull these fields: [LIST YOUR FIELDS: date, sender, subject, and whatever needs to be extracted from the body, saying exactly how it appears. E.g.: the order number is the digits after the hash in the subject; the amount is the number that appears after the word Total in the body.]
3) Write a new row at the end of the tab called [EXACT NAME OF YOUR TAB], with the columns in this exact order: [PASTE YOUR HEADERS SEPARATED BY SLASHES]
4) Apply the Gmail label "processed" to that message as soon as the row is written, creating the label itself the first time if it doesn't exist.
5) Before writing each row, check that message's ID isn't already in the "Message ID" column. If it already is, skip that message without writing anything.
6) Process at most 20 messages per run, so it doesn't hang.
7) If a field doesn't appear in the email, write an empty cell and keep going, without stopping the whole process.
8) Log how many messages it found, how many it wrote, and how many it skipped.

Mandatory rules:
- One single file, one main function called importEmails.
- No external libraries or advanced Google Cloud services.
- Use the minimum permissions necessary. If there's a way to do it without permission to delete email, use it.
- A comment above each block explaining what that part does.

After the code, and separately, give me: a) the numbered steps to run it by hand the first time; b) the list of permissions Google will ask for, translated into what they actually mean; c) the three most likely error messages the first time and what to do about each.
tasks.expect: A code block of 30 to 70 lines with comments, pasted into the editor and saved. At the top, in the function dropdown, "importEmails" should appear.
tasks.stuck: Do you get a red error at the bottom when saving, like "SyntaxError"? It's almost always that you also copied the triple-backtick line from the code block. Delete it. If the function dropdown shows up empty, the file wasn't saved. Press Ctrl+S again and wait for the "Unsaved" notice to disappear.

tasks.title: Get through the permissions screen without backing off
tasks.where: In the Apps Script editor, at the "Run" button up top
tasks.action: Check that the dropdown next to it says "importEmails" and click "Run." A window opens saying "Authorization required." Click "Review permissions" and pick your account, the same one that receives the emails. Here's the screen that's scary: "Google hasn't verified this app." Don't close it. Click "Advanced" at the bottom left, then the small link "Go to Order importer (unsafe)." Now Google shows you the list of permissions. Actually read it, don't skim it. If your script only reads emails and sends none, nothing about sending on your behalf should appear. If something doesn't add up, close and have the AI redo it with fewer permissions. If it checks out, click "Allow."
tasks.expect: The window closes on its own. A black panel appears below the editor with two lines: "Execution started" and "Execution completed," each with a timestamp. If your script logs anything, you'll also see how many emails it found.
tasks.stuck: If "Advanced" doesn't appear, widen your browser window: it hides in narrow windows. If you see "Access blocked: this app doesn't comply with Google's policy," you're on a work or school account. Its admin blocks personal scripts. Ask whoever administers the domain, or do it with your personal Gmail account. If you see "Error: you do not have permission to call GmailApp.search," you authorized with a different Google account than the one you were using. Sign out of all but the right one and run it again.

tasks.title: Check the result and trigger the bug on purpose
tasks.where: In your spreadsheet and the editor's "Executions" tab
tasks.action: Go back to the sheet: rows should have appeared. Count them and compare against the emails in Gmail matching your search. Now trigger the bug: go back to the editor and click "Run" again, without changing anything. This is the moment of truth. If the script is built right it shouldn't write a single new row, because the emails already carry the "processed" label. If the same rows show up again, the script isn't marking what's processed, and you've got the bug that sinks everyone. Delete the duplicate rows by hand. Go back to the AI with the message in the next section before setting up any trigger. A bug that repeats every ten minutes stops being a bug: it becomes three thousand rows.
tasks.prompt:
This script is writing duplicate rows every time I run it. I'm pasting the full code below.

Do this in this order:
1) Tell me in one sentence why it's duplicating, no jargon.
2) Fix it with TWO safeguards at once, not one: (a) apply the Gmail label "processed" to the message right after writing the row, and have the search exclude that label with -label:processed; (b) before writing, check whether the message's ID is already in the "Message ID" column of the sheet, and if it is, skip that message.
3) Give me back the whole corrected file, ready to paste over the old one. Don't give me just the changed part: I wouldn't know where to put it.
4) Tell me what I should see in the log when I run it twice in a row to know it's fixed.

Here's my code:
[PASTE THE WHOLE CODE HERE]
tasks.expect: On the second run, zero new rows. And a log message like "Found 0 messages" or "Found 12, wrote 0, skipped 12." That's exactly what you want to see.
tasks.stuck: If the "processed" label doesn't show up in Gmail, look right in Gmail. It's in the left sidebar: click "More" to expand the labels below. Does the script write rows but not apply the label? It's almost always because it applies it at the very end and something breaks before it gets there. Have the AI apply it right after writing the row, not after the loop finishes.

tasks.title: Set up the trigger and configure the failure alert
tasks.where: In the Apps Script editor, clock icon on the left sidebar
tasks.action: Click the clock ("Triggers") then the blue "Add Trigger" button at the bottom right. Fill in: function to run, "importEmails"; event source, "Time-driven"; type of time-based trigger, "Minutes timer"; interval, "Every 10 minutes." And now the thing almost nobody fills in, which is the most important part of the screen: at the bottom there's "Failure notification settings." Set it to "Notify me immediately." Without that, the day this breaks you won't find out. The worst thing about an automation isn't that it fails. It's that it fails silently for three weeks while you assume the orders are in the sheet. Save. Every ten minutes, day and night, even with your computer off.
tasks.expect: A row in the trigger list with the function, "Minutes timer," and "Every 10 minutes." Ten minutes later, in the "Executions" tab, a new line with status "Completed" and type "Time-driven."
tasks.stuck: If you see red "Error" in "Executions," click it and you'll get the full message. Copy it all and paste it to the AI saying "here's the error, here's my code, fix it and give me back the whole file." If no execution shows up after fifteen minutes, the trigger was saved under a different account. Delete the trigger, check top right which account you're on, and create it again.

tasks.title: Create the Slack doorbell and save it like a password
tasks.action: Log in with your workspace's Slack account. Click "Create New App" and choose "From scratch." Give it a name that'll look good in front of your coworkers, since it'll sign the messages: "Form Alerts," not "test2." Pick the workspace and create it. In the left menu click "Incoming Webhooks" and flip the switch at the top to "On." Scroll down and click "Add New Webhook to Workspace": it'll ask which channel. Pick a test channel, not the company-wide one. If you don't have one, create #testing before continuing. Copy the address that appears: it starts with https://hooks.slack.com/services/. Save it in your password manager, not in Notepad or an email to yourself. That address is the entire credential.
tasks.expect: A line like https://hooks.slack.com/services/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. And, in the channel you chose, an automatic Slack message saying an integration was added.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see "Create New App" or the button is grayed out, your workspace has app installation restricted. The screen offers you a button to ask an admin for permission. You can't continue until they approve it. If the channel dropdown doesn't show a private channel, it's because you're not a member: join the channel first and reload the page.

tasks.title: Connect the form to Slack and do a test submission
tasks.where: In your Google Form's response sheet, under Extensions and Apps Script
tasks.action: Open your form and go to the "Responses" tab. Click the green spreadsheet icon to link it to a sheet (if it's already linked, open that sheet). From that sheet, "Extensions" and "Apps Script" again. Paste the code the prompt below gives you, with your webhook address inside. Then, under the "Triggers" clock, add a new one: function "notifySlack," event source "From spreadsheet," event type "On form submit." Save, accept the permissions like before, and fill out the form yourself with fake data: "Name: test, Email: test@test.com." The message should reach Slack before you have time to switch tabs.
tasks.prompt:
You're an expert Google Apps Script programmer. You're writing for someone who has never coded before.

I have a Google Form whose responses land in this spreadsheet. I want a message to reach Slack via an incoming webhook every time someone submits the form.

The form has these questions, in this exact order:
[LIST YOUR QUESTIONS EXACTLY AS WRITTEN ON THE FORM]

I want the Slack message to look like this:
[WRITE HOW YOU WANT THE MESSAGE TO READ, using brackets for where each answer goes. E.g.: New trial class booking — [Name] ([Phone]) wants to come on [Preferred day]. Comment: [Comment]]

Requirements:
- One single function called notifySlack that receives the form event and reads the answers from that specific submission, not from the sheet's last row.
- The webhook address as a constant at the top of the file, with a comment clearly stating it's a secret and shouldn't be shared.
- If an answer comes back empty, write "(not answered)" instead of leaving an odd gap.
- Send the message correctly even with accented characters or emojis, without garbled text.
- If Slack responds with an error, log it with the exact code and text, instead of failing silently.
- Also add a separate function called testSlack that sends a fixed test message, so I can check the webhook without filling out the form.

After the code, tell me step by step which trigger I need to create in Apps Script for this to fire on form submit, with the exact name of each dropdown.
tasks.expect: A message in your Slack channel signed with your app's name. It arrives with the fake data you just typed, in under five seconds. In the editor's "Executions," a "Completed" line with type "On form submit."
tasks.stuck: If the log shows "returned code 400" with the word invalid_payload, the message format is built wrong. Paste the full error to the AI and have it redo it. If it shows "404" with no_service, the webhook was deleted or the app was uninstalled from the workspace. Go back to api.slack.com/apps and generate another one. If the message lands in a different channel than expected, that's not your mistake. Every webhook is bound to the channel you chose when creating it, and that can't be changed from the code. Create another webhook pointed at the right channel.

tasks.title: Write down the off switch before you leave
tasks.where: In a document of yours, and at myaccount.google.com/permissions
tasks.action: Write four lines in a document you'll be able to find six months from now. The four: where the script is (the sheet's link), what trigger it has and how often, which Slack channel it posts to, and how to turn it off. Turning it off means: opening the editor, clock icon, three dots to the right of the trigger, "Delete trigger." And to cut off access to your account entirely, go to myaccount.google.com/permissions. Find your project by the name you gave it and click "Remove Access." Do one more thing: go there now, even if you're not removing anything, and look through the whole list. You'll find apps you gave email access to back in 2019 that you don't even remember. Revoke those.
tasks.expect: A four-line document and your Google account's permissions screen open. Your project shows up in the list with the name you gave it.
tasks.stuck: If you don't recognize your project's name in the permissions list, you left it as "Untitled project." Go back to the editor, rename it top left, and reload the permissions page. If you accidentally revoke access from the script you just built, you haven't broken anything. The next run will error out: run it by hand once and reauthorize.

matters: Marking things as processed the instant you process them. This is the difference between an automation and a machine that generates garbage. Without that mark, a script running every ten minutes writes the same order 144 times a day. Within three days you have a sheet you no longer trust, which is worse than having no sheet.

Setting "Notify me immediately" on the trigger. A broken automation makes no noise: it just keeps not writing anything while you keep believing it's working. The email alert costs one click. It's the only thing that separates finding out today from finding out when a customer calls asking about their order from three weeks ago.

Treating the Slack webhook address like a password. It has no username, no login, and no record of who used it. Knowing it means being able to post in your channel. Make sure it never ends up in a forum screenshot or pasted into an AI chat. Anyone who sees it can send messages that look like they're from you.

Reading the permissions list before clicking "Allow," not the scary red screen next to it. The "unverified" screen only says Google hasn't reviewed your script. The permissions list says what it'll be able to do with your email for years to come. A script that only reads has no reason to ask to delete.
ignore: Setting up n8n on your own server with Docker. It's the most powerful option and the one every video shows. It's also the one that gets you spending a Saturday getting a container to start instead of connecting your two apps. Come back the day you have fifteen live automations.

Automatic retries, queues, and growing wait times. They matter when the other service goes down and you need to retry without hammering it. With a trigger that runs every ten minutes you already get retries for free. If it failed this time, it tries again on its own in ten minutes.

The real Gmail API, with its own Google Cloud project, its OAuth credentials, and its consent screen. That's what you'd need if you were building a product for other people. Apps Script saves you those six steps because it already lives inside your account.
canDo: Write the entire Apps Script script for you and get it right the first time if you give it the exact tab and column names. It's one of the things it does best: short, common, and heavily documented code.

Translate the errors for you, which is where the most time gets wasted alone. You paste it "Exception: Request failed for https://hooks.slack.com returned code 400" and it tells you the message is malformed. Not that your webhook is broken, which is what you'd have assumed.

Turn a sentence into the exact Gmail search. You say "the store's order emails that have an invoice attached and I haven't looked at." It gives you back from:orders@myshop.com has:attachment -label:processed newer_than:7d, with every piece explained.

Design the Slack message format and the sheet's column order for you. It does it better than you would off the top of your head. It's seen thousands and knows what reads well on a phone at eight in the morning.
cantDo: It can't click "Allow" for you. Google's permissions screen sits behind your password on purpose, and only your finger can click it. Same for creating the Slack webhook.

It can't see your Gmail or your sheet. When it tells you "I've checked and the script is now saving rows correctly," it's making that up. It hasn't checked anything, because it has no way to look. The only one who can look is you, in the "Executions" tab.

It doesn't know what's written inside your emails. If you ask it to pull "the amount," it has to guess where it is. If you paste it a real email with the data swapped, it gets it right. The difference between it working and not usually comes down to that sample email.

It can't undo what's already gone out. The 300 duplicate rows get deleted by hand. Messages that slipped into the company-wide channel can be deleted, but the notification already pinged forty phones. That's why you test in a separate sheet and a #testing channel.
words: Trigger
The event that starts the connection: an email arriving, someone submitting a form, it being nine in the morning. Without it, nothing moves on its own.
Action
What happens at the end of the connection: writing a row, sending a message, creating a task. It's the visible part, the one you check to know it went well.
Webhook

A long, secret internet address that works like a doorbell: whoever knows it can send a notification to that app from anywhere. Knowing it is all the permission needed, so it's stored like a password.
Polling
Going to check every few minutes whether something happened, instead of waiting to be notified. It works just as well, but what happens at 10:01 you don't see until 10:10.
OAuth
The "log in with your Google account" system applied to programs. Instead of giving your password to anyone, you approve a screen. The program is handed a pass you can revoke whenever you want.
Scope
The specific list of things a program will be able to do with your account: read email, write to your sheets, delete messages. It's what shows on the screen almost nobody reads before accepting.
Idempotent
Doing it ten times leaves the same result as doing it once. It's the property that stops your sheet from ending up with the same row repeated a hundred and forty times.
Execution log
The list of every time your automation has run. It shows the time, how long it took, and whether it finished fine or broke. It's what you check, not the sheet, when something doesn't add up.
Apps Script
The place where a small piece of code lives inside your own Google account. It's attached to a spreadsheet or a form. It's free, nothing to install, and it runs with your computer off.
Quota

The usage ceiling a company lets you have for free: so many minutes running per day, so many sends per month. Once you cross it, it stops working until the next day, and you're almost never warned beforehand.
